event_info.event_description: Analyze for disclosures on global pandemic risks. Look for corporate language discussing widespread impacts like supply chain disruptions, labor shortages, remote work transitions, and fundamental shifts in consumer demand.

holistic_analysis: AVB’s 2023-02-24 filing squarely acknowledges that the COVID-19 pandemic, now within the 0-3-year ‘recent-event’ window, continues to pose both direct and secondary threats to virtually every facet of its multifamily business model.  The company frames the risk as ongoing and largely uncontrollable: public-health mandates can impair rent collection and eviction rights; shifting work-from-home patterns can drain demand; supply-chain blockages and labour illness can inflate costs and delay projects; and fee-waiver rules can immediately erode revenue.  Although the disclosure remains mostly qualitative (no dollar figures), the language is specific and granular, mapping the pandemic to concrete operational vectors—collections, construction, workforce, consumer demand and regulatory constraints.  Because these impacts are described as prospective, continuing and in some cases already observed (e.g., higher concessions during the pandemic), they represent live, non-remote risks.  Applying the Time Decay Principle, evidence from 2020-2023 can receive high scores (7-10) when the statement is specific and materially linked, while more generic or indirect references settle into the 4-6 range.  Mitigating language is minimal, so most snippets retain high net severity scores.

evidence_list.snippet: The national and global impacts of a pandemic, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, may present material uncertainty and risk with respect to our financial condition, results of operations and cash flows.

components.reason: Explicitly links COVID-19 to ‘material uncertainty and risk’.
Covers three core financial dimensions (condition, operations, cash flow).

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Direct statement of material risk across multiple financial metrics justifies a high score of 7.

evidence_list.snippet: State, local, and federal entities may impose restrictions, for varying times and to varying degrees, on our ability to enforce residents’ contractual lease obligations, and this may affect our ability to enforce all our remedies (such as pursuing collections and seeking evictions) for the failure to pay rent.

components.reason: Identifies concrete regulatory action (lease-enforcement restrictions).
Connects restriction to financial mechanism—rent collection and evictions.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Specific regulatory curbs tied to core revenue collection elevate this to a 7.

evidence_list.snippet: Consumers whose income has declined, who are working remotely or who cannot freely access neighborhood amenities like restaurants, may decide to live in a location other than our markets.

components.reason: Cites pandemic drivers (income decline, remote work, amenity shutdown).
Highlights potential loss of occupancy/demand in AVB’s target markets.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Specific demand-shift scenario but unquantified impact warrants a mid-level 5.

evidence_list.snippet: Demand from students and demand for corporate apartment homes may be negatively impacted by trends in remote learning and work, and the adoption of new online technologies.

components.reason: Targets defined customer segments (students, corporate housing).
Attributes decline to pandemic-era behavioural shifts (remote learning/work).

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Segment-specific demand risk tied to pandemic behaviours scores 5.

evidence_list.snippet: Various state, local and federal rules may require us, in some jurisdictions or for some properties, to waive late fees and certain other customary fees associated with our apartment rental business.

components.reason: Identifies mandatory fee waivers imposed by government pandemic response.
Direct revenue erosion (loss of late & other fees).

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Direct mention of forced revenue give-ups yields a strong 6.

evidence_list.snippet: Our properties may incur significant costs or losses related to shelter-in-place or stay-at-home orders, quarantines, infection, clean-up costs or other related factors.

components.reason: Lists multiple cost drivers directly stemming from pandemic measures.
Uses severity adjective ‘significant costs or losses’.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Multiple direct cost vectors and ‘significant’ wording justify a 6.

evidence_list.snippet: Supply chain constraints could cause delays in our construction and redevelopment activity, and inflation could cause our construction and operating costs to increase without a commensurate increase in our rental revenue.

components.reason: Identifies pandemic-linked supply-chain disruption affecting project timelines.
Highlights cost inflation squeezing margins.
Notes absence of matching revenue—direct profitability threat.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Operational delay plus margin compression yields a high score of 7.

evidence_list.snippet: Emergency orders shutting down non-essential businesses, limiting congregations of people, and requiring social distancing may at times disrupt our development and construction activity.

components.reason: Points to government shutdown orders linked to pandemic.
Connects directly to disruption of development pipeline.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Specific shutdown-driven disruption of build pipeline merits 6.

evidence_list.snippet: A disruption in the normal operations of our workforce, as well as the possibility of illness among our associates or a substantial portion of our workforce, could also adversely affect our operations.

components.reason: Acknowledges workforce illness risk (health impact).
Links to adverse operational effects.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Workforce health risk is important but less financially quantified, scoring 5.

evidence_list.snippet: Our results of operations in future periods may be impacted directly or indirectly by uncertainties such as the lingering effects of the COVID-19 pandemic (the "Pandemic") and the recent increases in inflation.

components.reason: States lingering pandemic effects as ongoing uncertainty for future periods.
Frames impact as both direct and indirect, widening scope.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Generic but forward-looking uncertainty tied to pandemic earns 5.

evidence_list.snippet: If the financial condition of our residents and commercial tenants deteriorates, and/or regulations that limit our ability to evict residents and tenants continue or are adopted in response to future developments related to the Pandemic, that may result in higher than normal uncollectible lease revenue.

components.reason: Combines resident credit risk with eviction moratoria.
Directly predicts higher uncollectible revenue—quantifiable earnings hit.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Clear revenue loss mechanism (bad debt) tied to pandemic justifies 7.

evidence_list.snippet: The Pandemic may also depress consumer demand for our apartments for a variety of reasons, including (i) if consumers decide to live in markets that are less costly than ours for one or more reasons, such as a decline in their income or remote working arrangements; (ii) consumers who would otherwise rent may seek home ownership; and (iii) ongoing downward pressures on demand for certain types of housing (e.g., corporate apartment homes) or by certain consumers (e.g., students or consumers who require seasonal job-related demand such as in the entertainment industry).

components.reason: Enumerates multiple demand-side downgrade drivers linked to pandemic.
Covers several tenant categories and behavioural shifts.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Multi-vector demand reduction scenario gives a solid 6.
